subject: polluted industrial river
title: What If a River Caught Fire? Cleveland's Did, 13 Times

scenes.text: What if a river caught fire? Cleveland's did. Not once. Thirteen times.
The Cuyahoga was so coated in oil and factory waste that it first burned in 1868. A 1912 fire killed five dock workers.
For decades nothing lived in it. No fish at all. A 1952 fire did over a million dollars of damage.
Then, June 22nd, 1969: a spark from a passing train lit the oil. The fireboat put it out in under 30 minutes.
It was the smallest fire of them all. But Time magazine ran it nationwide, and the country finally paid attention.
Within three years the US created the Environmental Protection Agency and passed the Clean Water Act. Today about 70 fish species live in that river.

description:
What if a river caught fire? Cleveland's Cuyahoga River burned at least 13 times between 1868 and 1969 because of oil and industrial waste on its surface; a 1912 fire killed five people and a 1952 fire caused over 1.3 million dollars in damage.
The small 1969 fire, out in 20 to 30 minutes, made national news and helped push the creation of the EPA and the Clean Water Act within three years. The river now holds about 70 fish species, and in 2019 Ohio declared some safe to eat.

first_comment: Nobody photographed the 1969 fire; the famous picture Time printed was from the 1952 blaze. Cleveland voters had already approved 100 million dollars to clean the river a year before. Which environmental what-if should we run through next?
